To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a single non-intrusive dose of methamphetamine applied in young adulthood induces a significant increase in the density of GABAAergic terminals in the prelimbic region of the medial prefronta cortex of the gerbil.

methamphetamine-induced neuroplasticity in the pre-frontal cortex of adult rodents involves a selective increase in the GABAergic innervational density of pyramidal cells, and that the GABAergic input is likely to play a major regulatory role in the adaptive plasticity of the prefrontal dopamine network.
a single dose (25 mg/kg) of methamphetamine applied at the age 90 days to adult gerbils induces a significant increase in the GABAergic innervations in the medial pre-frontal cortex.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how the adult mammalian central nervous systems can react to a variety of environmental and pharmacological stimuli.
the question of how the brain adapts itself to a single noninvasive drug challenge in the absence of any overt pathological signs of neurodegeneration or neuroinflammation.
the hypothesis that drug-induced neuroplastic changes in the prefronto-cortico-limbic system are a prerequisite for the development of drug-induced psychopathology and addiction.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the prefrontal GABAergic system is capable to react to a single dose of psychostimulant by an increased density of GABA-ergic terminals.
the prefrontal dopamine system is capable of mediating a specific and selective adaptive response of the central nervous system to environmental stimuli.
methamphetamine-induced neurotoxicity is not a single event, but a sequence of events.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the drug challenge of young adult gerbil brains leads to a significant increase of prefrontal GABAergic innervations.
a non-invasive single dose of meth-amphetamine is an appropriate stimulus for the activation of adaptive neuroplasticity in the adult gerbil prefrontal cortex.
methamphetamine-induced neuroplasticity in the prefontal cortex of gerbils is a complex process involving a sequence of gain and loss of GABAergic and dendritic spine densities.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the prefrontal region of the adult gerbil brain can be used as a model system for studying drug-induced plasticity.
a single dose methamphetamine is sufficient to trigger neuroadaptations within the prefrontal dopamine system that may contribute to the development of addiction and other psychopathologies.
the adult mammalian brain is capable of structural and functional plasticity, and that this plasticity is not restricted to the hippocampus and the visual cortex.
